title: Disney World – Orlando, Florida
excerpt: Planning Walt Disney World for a group? How the park bus loops work, which vehicle fits, and why a charter bus to Orlando beats splitting into cars.

heroImage.alt: A motorcoach waiting in the charter bus loop outside a Walt Disney World theme park entrance in Orlando, Florida

extraImage.alt: A group boarding a mini bus outside their Orlando hotel in early morning light before a full day in the parks

body.text: Walt Disney World is not one destination, it is six gated attractions, dozens of resort hotels and a shopping district spread across roughly forty square miles of Central Florida. That scale is exactly why a charter bus to Orlando makes so much sense for a group. The distance between Magic Kingdom and Animal Kingdom alone is further than many people drive to work, and every one of those transfers is a chance for somebody to get lost, get stuck in a parking lot, or get separated from the group.

Picture the alternative. Fourteen people land at Orlando International, pick up four rental cars, and immediately split into four separate navigation problems. Two cars end up in different parking lots. One driver spends the day worrying about the return time on the rental agreement instead of enjoying the trip. Now picture the same fourteen people walking out of baggage claim onto one vehicle, luggage underneath, a driver who already has the week's itinerary. That difference is most of what groups are actually buying.
This is the part first-time group planners underestimate. The four parks do not all work the same way, and the differences matter when you are moving forty-plus people on a schedule.

items: Magic Kingdom is the one to plan around. There is no direct guest road to the park gates. Vehicles arrive at the Transportation and Ticket Center and guests cross Seven Seas Lagoon by monorail or ferry. Build an extra thirty minutes into both the morning arrival and the evening departure, and confirm current motorcoach procedures with Disney when you book, since drop-off arrangements are reviewed periodically.

EPCOT, Hollywood Studios and Animal Kingdom all have direct parking with designated oversized-vehicle areas. Your driver will be directed to a bus lot rather than the general car lot, which is usually a shorter walk than the standard parking rows.

Disney Springs has structured parking garages and a separate bus drop area. It is the easiest evening stop of the whole resort for a coach, and a good choice for a final night when nobody wants another early rope-drop.

The water parks have far less bus capacity than the theme parks. If Blizzard Beach or Typhoon Lagoon is on your list, treat it as a drop-and-return rather than assuming the vehicle can wait on site all day.

body.text: Why a charter bus to Orlando beats the alternatives

Orlando is a rideshare-heavy city, and for two people that works fine. For a group it falls apart quickly. Surge pricing at park closing is brutal, because tens of thousands of people are trying to leave at once and every app in the resort area prices accordingly. Splitting a group of thirty across eight vehicles at park close, in the rain, after a fourteen-hour day, is the single most common thing group leaders tell us they will never do twice.

A chartered vehicle also solves the storage problem nobody thinks about until day two. Ponchos, strollers, souvenir bags, a change of clothes for the child who went on the water rides in the morning: all of it lives on the bus instead of in a locker you rented or a backpack somebody carried for nine hours.
Choosing the right vehicle for your group
Group size drives this decision more than budget does, because the wrong-sized vehicle costs you either money or comfort every single day of the trip.

items: Large groups of 40 or more: a full-size coach from our [motor coach fleet](/fleet/motor-coaches) seats up to 56 with luggage bays underneath, reclining seats, climate control and a restroom. For a family reunion or a church group doing a full week, this is the default.

Mid-size groups of 20 to 32: a [mini bus](/fleet/mini-buses) is easier to maneuver in resort-area traffic and gets you closer to entrances at some properties. It is the sweet spot for a corporate incentive trip or a school band.
Small groups of 10 to 14: a [sprinter van](/fleet/sprinter-vans) handles a leadership retreat or an extended family without paying for seats nobody sits in.
Youth and student groups: a [school bus](/fleet/school-buses) seats 28 to 60 and is often the most economical option when the itinerary is short-hop park transfers rather than long highway legs.

body.text: One of the real advantages of having your own vehicle is that Central Florida opens up. Kennedy Space Center is about an hour east and is a genuinely strong day for mixed-age groups. Tampa is roughly ninety minutes west if you want to add a Gulf beach day. Daytona Beach is about an hour northeast. None of these are practical on a resort shuttle, and all of them are straightforward when the vehicle is yours for the day.
Groups that build in one non-park day almost always report it was the best decision they made. Six consecutive theme park days is more exhausting than it sounds on paper, particularly in summer.

Central Florida summers are hot and humid, and afternoon thunderstorms are close to a daily event from June through September. They usually pass in under an hour, but they will soak a group waiting outside for a ride. Having a vehicle to retreat to changes the character of that afternoon completely. Hurricane season officially runs from the first of June to the end of November, and while direct impacts on Orlando are uncommon, it is worth carrying flexible plans in September and October.

Interstate 4 is the artery connecting the airport, the resort area and downtown, and it is reliably congested at rush hour. An experienced driver who knows the local alternates is worth a great deal on a tight schedule. Late January through early March, and again in the weeks after Labor Day, tend to be the most comfortable windows for both weather and crowds.

items: Book early. Spring break, Thanksgiving week and the stretch between Christmas and New Year are the hardest dates in the Orlando market, and coaches are committed months ahead.
Give your coordinator the full itinerary, including park hours and any dining reservations. Early entry and extended evening hours can shift a pickup time by ninety minutes.
Decide up front whether the vehicle stays on site or returns. Both work, but they price differently and the answer changes your flexibility.
Nominate one person as the group's point of contact with the driver. Groups that skip this step lose twenty minutes at every single pickup.
